content: Animals that are suspected to be ill or deceased should be approached and handled with extreme caution. It is strongly recommended that such animals be examined by a veterinarian to determine the cause of illness or death. Individuals who engage in outdoor recreational activities, such as hikers, campers, and others, in areas where plague is enzootic should take the following precautions: a) Avoid direct contact with sick or dead animals. b) Steer clear of rodent nests and burrows. c) Apply insect repellents containing N, N-diethyl-m-toluamide (DEET) to exposed skin and use repellents or appropriate insecticidal sprays on clothing. d) Treat accompanying pets with suitable insecticides to prevent flea infestations. Hunters should always wear protective gloves when handling dead animals to minimize the risk of exposure to infectious agents. Persons suspected of having pneumonic plague should be placed under respiratory droplet precautions for at least 48 hours after the initiation of antibiotic therapy. Individuals with confirmed cases of pneumonic plague should remain under droplet precautions until their sputum cultures return negative results. For patients in whom pneumonic plague has been ruled out, standard precautions are sufficient. Close contact (within approximately 5 feet) with individuals suspected of having pneumonic plague should be avoided unless necessary precautions are taken. Persons without direct exposure to infected individuals are unlikely to contract the disease but should still be monitored closely for any signs of illness. Routine bacteriologic work involving Yersinia pestis can be safely conducted in biosafety level 2 laboratories. The use of biological safety cabinets to contain aerosols generated unintentionally is an effective measure to prevent laboratory workers from becoming infected. Laboratory-associated cases of Y. pestis infection are rare and typically involve unusual exposures in clinical diagnostic laboratories or research facilities working with live Y. pestis. The Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) series is published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). It is available free of charge in electronic format and can also be obtained in paper format through a paid subscription.
